253.title: The body: its parts
253.hook: like a bag of mixed grain opened and looked at: hair, nails, teeth, skin (MN 10)
253.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, the first five parts (hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin) are traditionally taught to new monks and nuns at ordination; the contemplation of the thirty-two parts is recited and practiced to loosen vanity and craving.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sampajanna, clear knowing, and your line was even this: no part of the day left out. Day two hundred fifty-three.

Think how much of a day goes into what the body looks like. The mirror in the morning. The photo retaken four times. The comparison that slips in while scrolling. The body becomes one picture, judged good or bad. The Satipatthana Sutta does something different. It opens the body up, piece by piece, with the calm of a farmer checking stored grain.
screen: `THE MIRROR, THE RETAKEN PHOTO.` → `ONE PICTURE, JUDGED.` → `PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: The practitioner reviews this very body, the sutta says, from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin and, in the sutta's blunt word, full of many kinds of impurity. Then the list: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and on inward, organs and fluids, thirty-one parts in the sutta's list. Later tradition added the brain to make thirty-two. Then the image. A bag with an opening at both ends, full of mixed grain: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, sesame, husked rice. A person with good eyes opens it and looks: this is rice, these are beans, this is sesame. Notice the tone. They aren't disgusted, and they aren't admiring. They're just sorting, clearly. That's the heart of the practice. In the Buddhist tradition, this contemplation is used to loosen two strong pulls: vanity about the body and craving for other bodies. Some teachers stress the unattractiveness of the parts; others, especially today, stress simple, neutral seeing. Either way, the point is not to hate the body. It's to see it as it is: not a single image to be judged, but a working collection of many things, each doing its job. Hair is hair. Teeth are teeth. The picture in the mirror loosens its grip a little.
screen: `FROM THE SOLES UP, THE HEAD DOWN.` · `HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.` · `A BAG OF MIXED GRAIN, OPENED.` · `SORTING, NOT JUDGING.` · then, large: `A BAG OF GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Name ten parts of your body slowly, feeling each one if you can: hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, muscles, heart, lungs, blood, breath. No admiring or wincing, just the calm of someone sorting grain: this is that. If any part is painful or hard to think about today, skip it gently and move on.
The body, its parts. Opened like a bag of mixed grain and sorted calmly: hair, nails, teeth, skin, each one just what it is.
Your line: a bag of grain. Sorted, not judged: each part just what it is. Day two hundred fifty-three.

254.title: The body: elements
254.hook: like a butcher who has divided a carcass: earth, water, fire, air (MN 10)
254.howItsDone: Meditators in several Buddhist traditions practice elements meditation by feeling hardness, cohesion, heat and motion in the body; in some Burmese and Thai lineages it is a core practice for seeing the body as not-self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, its parts, sorted like a bag of grain, not judged. Day two hundred fifty-four, and the body again, from a new angle.

Put your hand flat on a table. Feel the hardness under your palm. Now the warmth of your own hand, and maybe a slight dampness. Then the tiny movements: the pulse, the breath shifting your shoulders. Hard, wet, warm, moving. Those four make an old way of sorting what a body is made of, and the Satipatthana Sutta uses them to look at the body from one more angle.
screen: `HARD, WET, WARM, MOVING.` → `AN OLD WAY OF SORTING.` → `THE BODY AS ELEMENTS.`

segments.voice: The practitioner reviews this very body, however it is placed, however it is disposed, by way of the elements. In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element. Each is a dhatu, an element, and in Buddhist teaching they're less like substances, more like qualities you can feel. Earth is hardness and solidity: bones, teeth, the weight in your seat. Water is cohesion and fluidity: blood, sweat, the way things hold together. Fire is heat: warmth, digestion, the burn of a fever. Air is movement: the breath, the pulse, the push and pull inside. Then the image, and it's a blunt one. A skilled butcher, or his apprentice, has killed a cow and divided it at a crossroads, and sits with it cut into portions. The commentaries explain the point: before, he thought of it as a cow; now he sees only portions of meat. The name has fallen away, and what's left is just what's there. Looking at the body by elements does the same to the word me. Instead of a single, solid self, you find hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that are in the table, the rain, the sun and the wind. It isn't meant to be cold. Some practitioners describe it as a relief: the body is made of the world, and belongs to it.
screen: `DHATU: EARTH, WATER, FIRE, AIR.` · `QUALITIES YOU CAN FEEL.` · `THE BUTCHER AT THE CROSSROADS.` · `THE BODY IS MADE OF THE WORLD.` · then, large: `FOUR ELEMENTS.`

segments.voice: Feel earth, the solid seat and the weight of your hands; water, the moisture in your mouth and the way the body holds together; fire, the warmth of your hands or a cool spot on your skin; air, the breath moving and the pulse if you can find it. Then rest in all four at once, solid, fluid, warm, moving, and let the word me soften a little.
The body, elements. Earth, water, fire and air: hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that make up the world.
Your line: four elements. Even a sip from a cup holds all four. Two hundred fifty-four days now.

255.title: The body: the charnel ground
255.hook: a body one day dead, two days, three; this body too is of that nature (MN 10), offered gently
255.howItsDone: Reflection on death (maranasati) is practiced in many Buddhist traditions; some monastics use a skeleton or images of the stages, and lay practitioners often reflect quietly that this body, too, will not last.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body as four elements, earth, water, fire and air, the same four that make up the world. Day two hundred fifty-five, the last exercise on the body.

A quick word before today. The last body exercise in the sutta is about death, and it's direct. If you're grieving right now, or today just isn't the day, it's completely fine to listen lightly, or to spend the practice with your breath instead. Nothing is lost. For everyone else: it's easy to live as if one's own body were the one exception. Other people get old. Other people die. Somehow, not quite me. The sutta asks for a gentle, honest look at that.
screen: `A GENTLE NOTE FIRST.` → `THE ONE EXCEPTION.` → `THE CHARNEL GROUND.`

segments.voice: In the sutta's world, a charnel ground is a place where bodies were left out in the open, and the texts picture monks going there to practice. The sutta describes a practitioner who sees a body there: one day dead, two days, three. Then, over nine stages, it follows what happens next, until only scattered bones remain, bleached white, and finally bones crumbled to dust. At each stage the practitioner turns to their own body and reflects: this body too is of the same nature. It will become like that. It is not exempt. The whole exercise rests on that line: this body too. It sounds grim, but look at what it's for. It isn't meant to frighten, or to make life feel worthless. In Buddhist teaching, remembering death, maranasati, is meant to wake you up to what matters. The Buddha is remembered as saying that mindfulness of death, well practiced, is of great fruit. If this body won't last forever, a postponed phone call matters. An old grudge weighs more than it's worth. And an ordinary morning is precious, exactly because it's passing. Some practitioners say this reflection, done gently, leaves them calmer, not sadder. And the chorus comes back even here: arising and passing away, in the body itself.
screen: `A CHARNEL GROUND OUTSIDE TOWN.` · `NINE STAGES, DOWN TO DUST.` · `IT IS NOT EXEMPT.` · `REMEMBERING DEATH WAKES YOU UP.` · then, large: `THIS BODY TOO.`

segments.voice: Feel your body breathing, alive, warm, working, and quietly, if it feels right, reflect: this body too will not last forever. Let the thought be soft, not frightening, then ask one question, given that, what matters today, and let an answer come, or not. If this feels too heavy right now, just rest with the breath instead.
The body, the charnel ground. Seeing another body return to dust, the practitioner reflects: this body too is of that nature.
Your line: this body too. Not to frighten, but to show what matters. Day two hundred fifty-five, done.

a ritual for honoring ancestors' graves
a belief that flesh is evil and must suffer

256.title: Feelings
256.hook: pleasant, painful, neither; worldly and unworldly (MN 10)
256.howItsDone: Many insight meditation teachers have students note the feeling tone of experiences as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, since Buddhist teaching places vedana just before craving in the chain of dependent origination.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, the charnel ground, and your line: this body too. Day two hundred fifty-six, and the second foundation.

Buddhist teachers point to a moment that comes very fast: before a thing is even named, it already feels good, bad, or neither. A song starts, and before its name comes to mind, something may already have leaned in or pulled back. A smell drifts out of a kitchen: yes, or no. A text lights up your phone, and there's a little flicker of good or bad before you've read a word. That flicker is easy to miss, and in the Buddha's teaching it steers what comes next. The Satipatthana Sutta makes it the second foundation.
screen: `BEFORE YOU KNOW WHAT IT IS.` → `A FLICKER: YES OR NO.` → `THE SECOND FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: Vedana is usually translated feeling, but it doesn't mean emotions like joy or anger. It means the feeling tone of any experience: pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. In Buddhist teaching, every sight, sound, smell, taste, touch and thought comes with one of the three. The instruction is simple. Feeling a pleasant feeling, the practitioner knows, I feel a pleasant feeling. Feeling a painful one, they know it. Feeling one that's neither, they know that too. Then a second layer: each feeling can be worldly or unworldly. Worldly feelings are tied to ordinary things, like the pleasure of good food or the pain of an insult. Unworldly ones come from practice itself: the quiet joy of a calm mind, or the ache of wanting to be free. Then the chorus: inside, outside, arising and passing away. Why a whole foundation? Because in Buddhist teaching, feeling is the hinge. In the chain the Buddha called dependent origination, feeling gives rise to craving. Pleasant feeling tends to spark wanting more. Painful feeling tends to spark pushing away. Neutral feeling, the texts say, has ignorance lying behind it: it slips past unnoticed, and attention drifts off. Catch the feeling while it's still just a feeling, before it becomes a want or a push, and you've found a gap. In that gap, you get a choice.
screen: `NOT EMOTION: FEELING TONE.` · `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.` · `WORLDLY AND UNWORLDLY.` · `FEELING IS THE HINGE TO CRAVING.` · then, large: `PLEASANT, PAINFUL, NEITHER.`

segments.voice: Let your attention move around the body and the room, and each time something catches you, a sound, an ache, the warmth of your hands, a thought, give it one quiet label: pleasant, painful, or neither. Don't explain it or change it; just label it and let it go. You may notice how many things are simply neither, and that's normal.
Vedana. The feeling tone of every experience: pleasant, painful, or neither. The hinge between what happens and what we want.
Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Three tones, running under everything you meet. See you tomorrow.

a strong emotion like joy, anger, fear or grief

it means feeling tone: pleasant, painful, or neither.

that's why catching the feeling opens a gap.

original.note: Pali vedanā: feeling tone, pleasant, painful or neither.

what a scholar hears: in the twelve links of dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda), contact conditions vedanā, and vedanā conditions taṇhā, craving.

257.title: The second arrow
257.hook: pain is one arrow; the distress we add is a second (SN 36.6)
257.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers of many schools use the two arrows image from the Sallatha Sutta, and versions of it appear in some pain-care and mindfulness courses to separate physical pain from the distress added to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vedana, feeling tone. Your line: pleasant, painful, neither. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

You stub your toe on the bed frame at night. There's the pain, sharp and real. And then, within a second: who put this bed here, why am I so clumsy, this always happens to me, now I'll never get back to sleep. The toe hurt for thirty seconds. The rest of it went on for twenty minutes. The Buddha gave a short teaching about exactly this, with a picture from the battlefield.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT NIGHT.` → `THIRTY SECONDS OF PAIN.` → `TWENTY MINUTES OF THE REST.`

segments.voice: It's in the Connected Discourses, a sutta called the Arrow. The Buddha asks his monks: when an ordinary person and a well-trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference? Then he answers with an image. An untrained person, touched by a painful feeling, worries, grieves, laments, beats their chest and becomes distraught. It's as if they were struck by an arrow, and then by a second arrow right after. They feel two pains: one in the body, one in the mind. The well-trained disciple, touched by the same painful feeling, doesn't add the worry and the lament. They are struck by one arrow, not a second: they feel the bodily pain, and not the other. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say the trained person feels no pain. The first arrow lands on everyone, including, other texts say, the Buddha himself, who had back pain and grew old. The teaching is only about the second arrow, the one a person fires at themselves. And he adds something sharp. When pain comes, the untrained person often runs toward sensual pleasure to escape it, because they know no other way out. That's a third trap, hidden inside the second. It links straight back to yesterday. Pain is a feeling, vedana. The second arrow is what comes next. See the feeling as just a feeling, and the second arrow never leaves the bow.
screen: `THE ARROW SUTTA.` · `STRUCK BY ONE, THEN BY A SECOND.` · `THE FIRST ARROW LANDS ON EVERYONE.` · `THE SECOND IS THE ONE WE FIRE.` · then, large: `ONE ARROW, NOT TWO.`

segments.voice: Find some small discomfort, a stiff knee, an itch, a tight shoulder or a worry you've been carrying, and feel the first arrow: just the raw sensation, or the plain fact. Then watch for the second arrow, the story, the complaint, the why me, and when it comes, name it quietly: second arrow. Return to the first, and let it be only what it is.
Salla. The Pali word for an arrow: the first one is the pain itself, which lands on everyone; the second, which we fire ourselves, is the one to watch for.
Your line: one arrow, not two. The first lands on everyone; the second is the one to watch. That's day two hundred fifty-seven.

a bow, the Buddha's image for discipline

258.title: The mind
258.hook: a mind with lust or without, with hate or without, contracted or scattered (MN 10)
258.howItsDone: In contemplation of mind, practitioners periodically note the overall quality of the mind, such as agitated, calm, dull or clear, including the absence of a state, without trying to change it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salla, the second arrow. Your line was one arrow, not two. Day two hundred fifty-eight, and the third foundation.

Someone asks how you are, and you say fine. But what's the weather in there, really? Foggy? Stormy? Bright but a little windy? It's easy to be so busy with what's on the mind, the email, the argument, the list, that the mind itself goes unnoticed: its mood, its shape, its temperature. Like reading every word on a page without ever noticing the color of the paper. The third foundation in the Satipatthana Sutta asks you to notice the paper.
screen: `'FINE.' BUT WHAT'S THE WEATHER?` → `WHAT'S ON THE MIND, NOT THE MIND.` → `NOTICE THE PAPER.`

segments.voice: Citta is the Pali word for mind, or heart; the tradition doesn't split them the way English does. The sutta gives a list of pairs, and for each one the instruction is the same: know it. A mind with lust, know it as a mind with lust. Without lust, know it as without. With hate, or without. With delusion, or without. Then a contracted mind, pulled in and sluggish, or a scattered one, flying in all directions. An exalted mind, lifted by deep meditation, or one that isn't. A surpassable mind, or unsurpassable. A concentrated mind, or not. A liberated mind, or not yet. Sixteen states in all, in eight pairs. Two things stand out. First, the good states are on the list too. A calm mind is known as calm, not only an agitated one as agitated. This isn't a search for faults. It's a weather report, sunny days included. Second, every pair includes the absence. A mind without anger is worth noticing. Anger gets noticed when it shows up; the quiet hour when it's gone rarely does. That noticing is its own small gladness. And the chorus returns: inside and outside, arising and passing away. Mind states come and go just like breaths. The fog lifts. The storm passes. And simply knowing the weather already changes how you stand in it.
screen: `CITTA: MIND AND HEART TOGETHER.` · `WITH LUST OR WITHOUT, HATE OR WITHOUT.` · `CONTRACTED OR SCATTERED.` · `NOTICE THE ABSENCE TOO.` · then, large: `KNOW THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Take three slow breaths, then ask: not what's on the mind, but what's it like right now? Tight or open, scattered or gathered, irritated or free of irritation, heavy or light: pick one plain word for it and hold that word lightly. Every so often, check again: has the weather shifted?
Citta. The mind and heart together: its states, its weather, known as they are, whether stormy or clear.
Your line: know the mind. Clear days count too, and so does a worry that's gone quiet. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

the list includes calm, concentrated and liberated minds too: a full weather report.
the sutta asks you to notice when anger is absent

259.title: Knowing without fixing
259.hook: you know an angry mind as angry: that is the whole instruction
259.howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often stress bare knowing of mind states, noting 'angry' or 'restless' without judgment, as the first step; remedies such as loving-kindness are taught separately.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was citta, the mind and heart, known like the weather. Your line was know the mind. Day two hundred fifty-nine, the end of another week in the sutta.

You notice you're anxious. Right away, a whole repair crew shows up. You should calm down. Why are you like this? Try breathing slower. Think positive. Fix it, fix it, fix it. And somehow the anxiety gets worse, now with frustration on top: anxious, and anxious about being anxious. Yesterday's list in the sutta had an instruction hiding in it, so simple it's easy to miss.
screen: `THE REPAIR CREW SHOWS UP.` → `'JUST RELAX.'` → `AN INSTRUCTION HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look again at the wording. A mind with anger: know it as a mind with anger. That's all. It doesn't say, then remove the anger. It doesn't say, replace it with kindness. It doesn't say, feel bad for being angry. In this section, the whole instruction is to know. Other teachings in the Buddhist tradition do give remedies, kindness for ill will, reflection on the body for lust, and those come later. But the Satipatthana Sutta puts something first: before you change anything, see it clearly. Why? Trying to fix a mind state usually means pushing against it, and pushing is its own kind of aversion. It's the second arrow again, aimed at your own moods. Knowing takes a step back. Say, this is an angry mind, and there's no longer just anger. There's also a knowing of the anger. There's a little space there, and in that space the anger can loosen by itself, the way a knot loosens when you stop pulling both ends. Look back over this week and the same move is everywhere. The parts of the body, sorted like grain. The elements, felt as they are. The charnel ground: this body too. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. The second arrow, not fired. The mind, known as the weather. Every one of them is seeing, not fixing. Six sections, one move.
screen: `A MIND WITH ANGER: KNOW IT.` · `SEE CLEARLY BEFORE CHANGING.` · `FIXING IS OFTEN PUSHING.` · `THE WEEK: SEEING, NOT FIXING.` · then, large: `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: Find whatever mood is here right now, restless, flat, content, tired, a little sad, and name it plainly: a restless mind. Instead of fixing it, stay with it the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If the urge to fix shows up, know that too, a mind that wants to fix: nothing to do but know.
Knowing. In this section of the sutta, the whole instruction for a mind state, angry or calm, is simply to know it, nothing more.
Your line: just know it. Seeing comes before changing. Another week in the sutta, done.

fork.reveal: the sutta says to know the mind as it is. seeing clearly comes before any change.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing without fixing means giving up on getting better.
what it means: seeing a state clearly first, so it can loosen on its own.
what a scholar hears: MN 10's mind section contains no remedies; remedies for unwholesome thoughts appear elsewhere, for example in MN 20, the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), contemplation of mind
